Banded archerfish (Toxotes jaculatrix) hatch from small pelagic eggs with a diameter of approximately 0.46 mm, which provides a calculated wet weight at birth of just 0.00005 grams [Wwb = 0.00005 grams]. This negligible initial mass reflects the extreme altricial state of the newly emerged yolk-sac larva, which depends entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the first days of life. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable water temperature of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C], the developmental period from egg fertilisation to hatching is consistently short, with the age at birth recorded as 4 days [ab = 4 days]. This rapid embryogenesis is typical of tropical teleosts that reproduce in warm, productive mangrove and brackish-water habitats where predation pressure on early life stages is intense. The newly hatched prolarva, measuring only a few millimetres, must quickly absorb its yolk and transition to exogenous feeding to sustain the accelerated growth trajectory that characterises the species.

As the young archerfish progresses through the larval and early juvenile phases, it undergoes a rapid increase in body length before reaching the critical milestone of pubertal development. Field surveys and captive-rearing studies consistently indicate that individuals attain a total length at puberty of approximately 10 cm [Lp = approximately 10 cm], a size that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of roughly 16.6 grams [Wwp = roughly 16.6 grams]. This size threshold marks the onset of gonadal maturation and the initial activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. The time since birth at puberty is reached at approximately 547.5 days [tp = approximately 547.5 days] when maintained at a water temperature of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C], a relatively protracted juvenile period that allows for substantial somatic growth and the development of the specialised oral morphology required for ballistic prey capture. The length-based maturation schedule is consistent with patterns observed in other toxotid species inhabiting similar estuarine environments.

The ultimate or asymptotic total length achieved by sexually mature individuals is 30 cm [Li = 30 cm], a value that represents the maximum size attained by this species under favourable environmental conditions. Corresponding to this maximum length, the ultimate wet weight reaches approximately 448 grams [Wwi = approximately 448 grams], a body mass that places Toxotes jaculatrix among the mid-sized members of its family. This adult body size is likely shaped by the constraints of its specialised feeding ecology, which requires both powerful jaw musculature and precise neuromuscular coordination for the characteristic water-jetting behaviour used to dislodge terrestrial prey. Large adults, particularly those occupying productive mangrove creeks, approach this asymptotic size after several years of continuous growth, with the rate of length increase tapering markedly as the fish approach their maximum recorded dimensions. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that the ultimate length is relatively conservative within the genus.

The maximum lifespan of Toxotes jaculatrix has been documented at 5 years [am = 5 years] under captive conditions maintained at a stable temperature of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C]. This longevity is relatively modest compared to some larger tropical teleosts, but it reflects the species' position as an iteroparous, multiple-spawning predator with a compressed reproductive window following the onset of maturity. The age at birth of 4 days [ab = 4 days] at the same thermal regime underscores the rapid pace of early development, while the overall life span of 1825 days [am = 1825 days] at 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C] encompasses the complete life history from embryonic stage through reproductive senescence. The combination of a short egg stage, a moderately long juvenile phase, and a total life span of several years is consistent with a life-history strategy that balances early mortality risk against the benefits of achieving a large adult body size capable of exploiting a specialised trophic niche.

Reproductive output in banded archerfish has been characterised through observations of captive spawning events, with females releasing a modest number of eggs per event. Spawning females typically produce approximately 1 to 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 1 to 3 eggs per clutch], and they may generate a single such clutch each year [F_R_i = single such clutch each year] during the protracted breeding season. This low fecundity per event, combined with the extended time since birth at puberty of 547.5 days [tp = 547.5 days] at 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C], indicates a life-history strategy oriented toward producing relatively large, well-provisioned eggs that yield robust larvae capable of surviving the challenging conditions of the mangrove nursery habitat. The total length at puberty of 10 cm [Lp = 10 cm] marks the transition to this reproductive life stage, after which individuals may spawn repeatedly over several consecutive years, contributing to the population's recruitment through a strategy of iteroparity that buffers against annual variation in environmental conditions.
